Respiratory Illness Outbreak Disrupts U.S. Machinery Industry, Production Resumes After Containment

A recent outbreak of a respiratory illness among workers in the U.S. machinery industry disrupted production at several major facilities nationwide, industry groups and company officials confirmed Tuesday. The illness, identified as a strain of adenovirus, prompted temporary closures and quarantines at seven manufacturing sites across the Midwest and Southeast over the past three weeks.

The National Association of Machinery Manufacturers (NAMM) reported that more than 380 workers contracted the virus, with most cases centered at PrecisionForge Inc. in Ohio and Allied Motion Systems in Tennessee. Company spokespersons said affected employees experienced flu-like symptoms, including fever, cough and shortness of breath. Local health authorities intervened after initial clusters were detected in late May.

"Protecting our workforce was our top priority," said Pamela Ortiz, Chief Operating Officer of PrecisionForge Inc. "We temporarily suspended operations for deep cleaning and provided paid leave to impacted employees. Fortunately, most cases were mild and all workers are now recovering."

State health departments coordinated with plant management to implement mass testing, contact tracing, and enhanced ventilation protocols. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there is no evidence of ongoing transmission at any site. Affected facilities have now resumed normal production schedules.

The disruption led to a reported 12% drop in machinery output in June, according to figures provided by NAMM. Industry analysts estimate this could result in delayed order fulfillment and minor supply chain backlogs through July.

"While the outbreak caused short-term challenges, prompt action and cooperation helped minimize long-term impacts," said NAMM president Charles Lee. "We’re closely monitoring the situation and advising members on continued preventive measures."

No fatalities were reported, and all affected workers are expected to return to work within the next week, officials said.
